text.font-family: 'Arial Unicode MS','Segoe UI Symbol','DejaVu Sans','Noto Sans Symbols 2',sans-serif

svg.text: Typhon is the Greek mythic embodiment of violent, chaotic natural power—a colossal serpentine or draconic being
associated especially with storms, destructive winds, volcanic fire, and cosmic rebellion.

text.font-family: 'Arial Unicode MS','Segoe UI Symbol','DejaVu Sans','Noto Sans Symbols 2',sans-serif

svg.text: 1. The priestess must become Hekate—she of many names and faces—in order to access the crossroads
(+): Earth runs horizontally, with paths descending to the Underworld and ascending to Ouranos. These three realms will take the
priestess to commune with one of Medea-Hekate’s many identities; her many identities will help her travel: Persephone taking the
path to the underworld, Aphrodite taking her to Ouranos, then seeking Artemis to go back to Earth, to use the three faces of her
training to invoke travel on the crossroads in order to access one of her identities.

text.font-family: 'Arial Unicode MS','Segoe UI Symbol','DejaVu Sans','Noto Sans Symbols 2',sans-serif

svg.text: 2. The biblical cross (+) may represent a crossroads: its horizontal axis signifies Earth, its upward vertical axis Ouranos (Heaven),
and its downward vertical axis Gaia (Underworld). This could reflect the same three-realm structure associated with Hekate and her
crossroads, suggesting a derived tradition or knowledge of that cosmology.

text.font-family: 'Arial Unicode MS','Segoe UI Symbol','DejaVu Sans','Noto Sans Symbols 2',sans-serif

svg.text: 3. The crucifix (+) hides the Christian mystery it was using from a previous tradition in plain sight, for eyes to see. Jesus can be
best understood in the context of the chthonic mother he was calling for while on the cross (Matthew 27:46; Mark 15:34).
This is the internal/hidden Christian mystery. He accomplished the keys to the mystery himself within the rite, described in
Revelation of John (Revelation 1:18: ἐγενόμην νεκρὸς … ἔχω τὰς κλεῖς τοῦ θανάτου καὶ τοῦ ᾅδου —
“I was dead … I hold the keys of Death and Hades”). Jesus told his followers after his catharsis chamber, that they too can
take the Snake Venoms: you too can pick up snakes (ophis) and drink the deathinducer (thanasimon), it will not harm them,
they'll be able to heal others, and be healed themselves (Mark 16:18).

text.font-family: 'Arial Unicode MS','Segoe UI Symbol','DejaVu Sans','Noto Sans Symbols 2',sans-serif

g.text: 4. An alternative older Pontic tradition defines Realms as [Sea, Heaven, Earth] instead of [Underworld, Heaven, Earth], but both are
equivalent (as Abyss or Void). Queen Amphitrite is the guide to Pontos (Sea), where queen Persephone is the guide to Hades
(Underworld). Medea comes from Colchis on the Pontic Sea; she directs Hekate’s rites on its coast. Incidentally, the Sea Peoples
migrated during the Late Bronze Age collapse. This may explain the regional ubiquity of the Hecatean / Orphic kosmology, in the
Greek and Roman empires. Hesiod, Theogony 411–427 (c. 700 BCE); Apollonius Rhodius, Argonautica 4.245–252 (3rd c. BCE); Orphic Hymn

text.font-family: 'Arial Unicode MS','Segoe UI Symbol','DejaVu Sans','Noto Sans Symbols 2',sans-serif

g.text: 5. Medea and Ammon. Medea (Μήδεια), Ammon’s (Ἄμμων) earliest priestess (citation needed). Pindar, Pythian 4.1–58 (462 BCE): Medea’s
prophecy concerning Libya and Zeus Ammon.

text.font-family: 'Arial Unicode MS','Segoe UI Symbol','DejaVu Sans','Noto Sans Symbols 2',sans-serif

g.text: 6. Diana, Dionysos and Bacchus. Diana and Dionysos: proposed linguistic connection. Dionysos is attested in Mycenaean Linear B as
di-wo-nu-so (PY Ea 102; KH Gq 5, Late Bronze Age). Bacchus (Βάκχος) comes to us from the Greek in the fifth-century BCE Berezan
dedication, SEG 32.745 ([Διονύ]σωι Βά[κχωι]), and the Olbian graffito Dettori 1996, 301a (BAKXO). Diana is the Roman/Italic goddess
historically identified with Greek Artemis, both represent the wild hunt on Earth.

text.font-family: 'Arial Unicode MS','Segoe UI Symbol','DejaVu Sans','Noto Sans Symbols 2',sans-serif

g.text: 7. The ritual formularies. The Greek and Egyptian Magical Formularies preserve a recurring ritual vocabulary of divine names,
multiple identities, φάρμακα, material preparations, invocations, and transformations. GEMF 15.419–432; GEMF 28.72–84; GEMF 57 / PGM

text.font-family: 'Arial Unicode MS','Segoe UI Symbol','DejaVu Sans','Noto Sans Symbols 2',sans-serif

g.text: 8. 7 Stars or Aions, give us relevant guidance as well. Plato, Republic 616c–617c; PGM XIII.24–26 (= GEMF 60); Revelation 1:4, 1:12,

text.font-family: 'Arial Unicode MS','Segoe UI Symbol','DejaVu Sans','Noto Sans Symbols 2',sans-serif

g.text: 9. behind every maenid is a satyr helping her find aphrodite; eunuchs are turned on/off for the domain of heaven (baselea of
ouranos). Jesus: Matthew 19:12. Satyrs are attested in Priapus’s company at a Bacchic gathering; Ovid, Fasti 1.391–440.

text.font-family: 'Arial Unicode MS','Segoe UI Symbol','DejaVu Sans','Noto Sans Symbols 2',sans-serif

g.text: 10. Despoina and the four goddess names. Despoina (δέσποινα, Mistress/Lady) is the title used in the Selene prayer, whose four linked
goddess identities are Selene/Mene, Hekate, Artemis, and Kore/Persephone: sea-born, night-roaming/night-crier, bull-faced/bull-eyed,
many-formed/three-formed, and poison-arrow-shooting (ios arrow poisons; ἰοβόλος). Kore is Persephone; Pausanias explicitly compares
the titles Despoina and Kore, although his Arcadian mystery account distinguishes the unnamed Arcadian Despoina, daughter of Demeter
and Poseidon, from Kore/Persephone, daughter of Demeter and Zeus. In royal language Medea, daughter of King Aeetes, is the
despoina/princess of Colchis. The Italian Bona Dea (“Good Goddess”) is likewise a protective title; Macrobius records an ancient
identification of Bona Dea with Medea because of her medicinal herbs and the exclusion of men from the sanctuary. PGM IV.2241–2358;
PGM IV.2785–2890; Pausanias 8.37.9; Apollonius Rhodius, Argonautica 3.241–244; Macrobius, Saturnalia 1.12.26.

text.font-family: 'Arial Unicode MS','Segoe UI Symbol','DejaVu Sans','Noto Sans Symbols 2',sans-serif

g.text: 11. Medea’s story is being told through Iphigenia and Andromeda. Euripides’ Medea invokes Hekate as the mistress she honors above all
and as her companion dwelling within (Medea 395–398). In Iphigenia among the Taurians, Artemis substitutes a deer for Iphigenia and
makes her priestess (28–30), while Athena later establishes her rites (1446–1467); the Hesiodic tradition explicitly says Iphigenia
became Hekate (Pausanias 1.43.1). Euripides’ lost Andromeda dramatized another bound maiden delivered from death (Euripides,
Andromeda, frs. 114–156 Kannicht; Aristophanes, Thesmophoriazusae 1010–1135). Through these two heroines, Medea’s story is retold as
the priestess becoming Hekate—or Hekate coming through Medea as her vessel.

text.font-family: 'Arial Unicode MS','Segoe UI Symbol','DejaVu Sans','Noto Sans Symbols 2',sans-serif

g.text: 12. Proof that Dionysis was older than the Bible: Greek Isaiah forbids the previous dionysian tradition; stop the treading of wine,
remove joy and rejoicing from the vineyards, and silence the 'vintage cry'. 'The vintage cry has ceased' (πέπαυται γὰρ κέλευσμα;
Isaiah 16:10 LXX). This suppressed vintage shout is highly relevant to Bacchic tradition: Euripides’ Bacchae portrays Dionysian
women bringing wine from the earth (Bacchae 704–711). Dionysos is already named in Mycenaean Linear B (PY Xa 102; KH Gq 5, c. 13th
century BCE), roughly a millennium before the Greek Septuagint Isaiah of the 2nd century BCE; this establishes that the Bacchic
tradition existed and was known far before the writing of YHWH, and was being suppressed by their newer cult.
